core_obligations: Show the intersection is contained in the maximal ideal: since the maximal ideal is not the generic point, some I in S is contained in it (proof lines 7353-7355).

For a nonzero f in the maximal ideal, use that V(f) is covered by the V(I) with I in S and that V(f) is quasi-compact in the constructible topology to extract a finite subcover V(I_1), ..., V(I_n) (proof lines 7356-7362).

Use closure of S under products to replace the finite family by the single ideal I_1 ... I_n, deduce I^m contained in (f) from finite generation, then I contained in (f^2) for some I in S, and conclude that f cannot be an element of that I, so f is not in the intersection (proof lines 7363-7367).
proof_roadmap: Contain the intersection in the maximal ideal (proof lines 7353-7355).
Convert the covering of V(f) into a finite subcover by constructible quasi-compactness (proof lines 7356-7362).
Collapse the finite subcover to one ideal, use the two power containments, and exclude f from the intersection (proof lines 7363-7367).
difficulty_reason: Let A be a local domain which is not a field and S a set of finitely generated ideals closed under products whose union of vanishing loci is the complement of the generic point; the lemma asserts that the intersection of all members of S is the zero ideal (statement lines 7343-7350). The proof is not a direct computation with the ideals but a compactness argument in the constructible topology: since the maximal ideal is not the generic point, some I in S is contained in the maximal ideal, so the intersection is contained in the maximal ideal; then for a nonzero f in the maximal ideal the closed set V(f) is covered by the V(I) with I in S, and quasi-compactness of V(f) in the constructible topology gives a finite subcover by V(I_1), ..., V(I_n) (proof lines 7353-7362). Because S is closed under products, the product I_1 ... I_n lies in S and V(f) is contained in V(I) for that single I; finite generation of I gives I^m contained in (f) for some m, closure under products gives I contained in (f^2) for some I in S, and then f cannot lie in that I (proof lines 7363-7367). Replacing a finite cover by one ideal through closure under products, and exploiting the two inclusions I^m subset (f) and I subset (f^2), is the non-formal content, so the claim is H2.
